Free, with no adverts, no network access, no data collected and no permissions requested.

Back in 2011 James Gittins put the fight itself on your home screen, and a lot of us left it running there for years. It stopped installing on modern Android long ago. This is not a port or a revival: no code and no asset is shared, and everything here was written from nothing. What carried over is the idea, and it deserved to still work. Thanks, James.

The movement, the timings and the creature values are read from the linuxdoom-1.10 source release, which is GPL-2.0 - and so, by obligation, is this app. Every such value carries a comment naming the file and the symbol it came from.

The artwork could not come from the same place. That source was released; the graphics that shipped with the game were not, and they are still somebody's copyright. So none of them are here, and nothing on this screen is drawn from them. Freedoom is the alternative, and it is an excellent one: every sprite, every colour, every floor you see is the Freedoom project's, made over twenty years by volunteers and given away to anyone who wants it. It is a complete game in its own right, not a stand-in for one. Without it there would be nothing to show, and it deserves to be played, not only borrowed from.

This project is independent. Neither the Freedoom project nor any other rights holder endorses or is involved in it.

The scene always thinks at the original 35 steps a second. The frame rate is only how often it is drawn, and it is the one setting here that changes battery use. Ten lasts longest on a charge, twenty is the smoothest, and twenty is where it starts.
